title: Postpartum Haemorrhage
recognize: Start the PPH bundle for measured blood loss ≥500 mL, or ≥300 mL with abnormal haemodynamics (WHO 2025); treat concerning ongoing bleeding/shock immediately without waiting for a volume threshold.
Assess pulse, BP, shock index, perfusion and consciousness repeatedly; concealed loss and baseline anaemia can mask severity.
A soft enlarged uterus suggests atony. Persistent bleeding with a firm uterus requires urgent assessment for trauma, retained tissue, inversion/rupture or coagulopathy.
callForHelp: Declare PPH, state time of birth and blood loss, and allocate a team leader, resuscitation/drug clinician and recorder.
Call senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, midwifery lead and blood bank together; activate the major-haemorrhage protocol early if bleeding/shock is substantial.
Prepare theatre, blood products and neonatal support; explain events to the patient/companion through a designated team member.

steps: Resuscitate and identify the cause IN PARALLEL: two large-bore IV cannulae, bloods/crossmatch and quantified cumulative loss; oxygen for hypoxia/shock, active warming and monitored fluid/blood replacement.
Massage the uterus and use bimanual compression for atony; empty the bladder with a Foley catheter and measure urine output.
Give oxytocin loading plus infusion and TXA using the complete cards below. Record previous prophylactic uterotonics: their identity changes the next uterotonic choice.

For ongoing ATONIC bleeding, choose an appropriate additional uterotonic now: avoid ergometrine/methylergometrine with hypertension or pre-eclampsia, and avoid carboprost with asthma/significant pulmonary disease. Do not give both ergot preparations as though they are interchangeable.
Keep examining the 4Ts while drugs are administered. Do not wait to finish eight carboprost doses before preparing tamponade or surgery in ongoing haemorrhage.

investigations: CBC/platelets, group and crossmatch, PT/APTT and fibrinogen; repeat during ongoing major loss and after replacement.
Blood gas/lactate, ionised calcium, potassium, temperature and renal function; results guide resuscitation but never postpone haemorrhage control.
Examine placenta/membranes and inspect cervix/vagina/perineum with adequate exposure/analgesia. Ultrasound can support assessment of retained tissue but must not delay treatment.

steps: TONE: continue bimanual compression and the selected uterotonics. TRAUMA: inspect and repair tears/haematoma; assess rupture/inversion. TISSUE: arrange skilled manual removal/evacuation when indicated; do not forcibly detach a suspected accreta placenta. THROMBIN: correct coagulopathy with the blood bank while obtaining source control.

If atony continues despite initial treatment, consider intrauterine balloon tamponade only after assessing trauma/retained tissue and where monitoring, blood and immediate surgical rescue are available. Use sterile technique, the specific balloon’s recommended filling fluid/volume and a drainage channel; record fill volume and continuing blood loss.

Bakri-type devices have a manufacturer-specific maximum volume (commonly 500 mL); do not inflate repeatedly beyond the device limit to compensate for persistent bleeding. Continue observations, uterotonic support and an explicitly prescribed antibiotic/removal plan.

Persistent bleeding, deteriorating physiology or a failed tamponade test means immediate senior operative control. Compression sutures/devascularisation, embolisation in a stable suitable patient, or hysterectomy are selected by cause and expertise; this is not a mandatory ladder requiring every step before hysterectomy.

escalation: Continuing loss or shock despite initial treatment: theatre and major-haemorrhage support immediately, without an arbitrary waiting period.
HDU/ICU for ongoing shock, vasopressor/ventilation need, coagulopathy, organ dysfunction or large transfusion; a unit count is not the sole admission criterion.

During transfer, continue uterine/aortic compression as appropriate, warming and blood/fluid support with skilled escort; contact the receiving team first. Compression/tamponade must not delay transfer or definitive rescue.
postEventCare: Continue close uterine-tone, bleeding, perfusion, urine-output and laboratory review until stable; document every product, drug and operative decision.
Correct iron deficiency/anaemia using the measured deficit and clinical status. Reassess VTE prophylaxis only after haemostasis and an anaesthetic/bleeding-risk review.
Explain the cause and treatment, offer psychological/lactation support, arrange Hb/clinical follow-up and a future-pregnancy delivery plan.

title: Eclampsia
recognize: New seizure during pregnancy after 20 weeks or postpartum: treat suspected eclampsia promptly while considering other causes. Normal BP or absent proteinuria does NOT exclude it.
Persistent altered consciousness, focal deficit, fever, head injury or recurrent seizures despite treatment requires urgent investigation for an alternative/additional diagnosis.
callForHelp: Activate obstetric emergency response with senior obstetrician, anaesthetist and resuscitation support; note onset and duration.
Bring magnesium, the correct infusion equipment, calcium gluconate and severe-BP medicines; neonatal team and theatre plan once the mother is stabilised.

steps: Protect from injury, left-lateral positioning, suction and airway support; do not restrain forcibly or place objects in the mouth. Check glucose immediately. Give oxygen for hypoxaemia and assist ventilation if needed.
Give ONE magnesium regimen from the cards: IV/IM OR IV maintenance, not both. Maintain a running magnesium dose/time record.
Treat persistent systolic ≥160 OR diastolic ≥110 mmHg promptly with the selected acute-BP sequence. Magnesium treats seizures; it does not replace antihypertensive treatment.
Assess reflexes, respiration and urine output throughout treatment. For toxicity: stop magnesium, support ventilation, call anaesthesia and give calcium gluconate as below.

investigations: CBC/platelets, creatinine/electrolytes, LFTs, urine protein and coagulation when indicated; bedside glucose immediately.

After maternal stabilisation, fetal assessment if undelivered. Neuroimaging/neurology for focal findings, prolonged coma, atypical timing or refractory seizures; do not delay resuscitation/Mg for imaging.

steps: Recurrent seizure: reassess airway, glucose and magnesium exposure/toxicity before the additional magnesium dose. Continued convulsions require anaesthetic/ICU support and a refractory-seizure plan.

Once maternal seizures, oxygenation and BP are controlled, plan birth irrespective of a reassuring gestational-age threshold; eclampsia is not managed by simply waiting until 34 weeks. Choose route by obstetric circumstances rather than automatic caesarean.
Continue the chosen magnesium regimen until 24 h after birth or the last seizure, whichever is later; individualise for renal dysfunction or toxicity.

escalation: Recurrent/prolonged seizures, inability to protect airway, hypoxia, pulmonary oedema, coma or organ failure: ICU/anaesthesia immediately.
Restrict maintenance fluids appropriately in severe pre-eclampsia, including drug-carrier volumes; titrate any resuscitation to clinical need and avoid fluid overload.
postEventCare: Continue neurological/respiratory, BP, urine-output and laboratory monitoring; reassess unexpected deterioration or persistent headache/visual symptoms.
Inform neonatal staff of maternal magnesium exposure. Plan postnatal antihypertensive review and long-term cardiovascular follow-up.

title: Acute Severe Hypertension (>=160/110)
recognize: Systolic ≥160 OR diastolic ≥110 mmHg persisting on prompt repeat measurement, generally within 15 min; do not wait 4 h to confirm an emergency.
Severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/right-upper-quadrant pain, dyspnoea, seizure or focal deficit indicates possible end-organ involvement.
callForHelp: Urgent senior obstetric and anaesthetic review; bring acute antihypertensive drugs and monitor BP/pulse.
Screen for severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia and alert the appropriate critical-care team for organ dysfunction.

steps: Choose an appropriate acute agent based on IV access, airway and comorbidity. Use the complete labetalol, hydralazine or swallowed immediate-release nifedipine sequence below; do not combine several loading sequences without tracking response and cumulative doses.

Avoid abrupt hypotension: reassess BP after each scheduled interval, aiming to leave the severe range promptly, then titrate to the chosen guideline’s ongoing target. Assess pulse and fetal condition.

Consider magnesium for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia according to the obstetric assessment; it is not a BP drug. Avoid routine fluid loading in pre-eclampsia unless clinically indicated.

investigations: CBC/platelets, creatinine/electrolytes, LFTs and proteinuria assessment; coagulation when indicated.
Assess symptoms, oxygenation and fluid balance; fetal monitoring as appropriate. Image for suspected stroke or another acute neurological cause.

steps: Persistent severe BP after the selected initial sequence requires senior review, an alternative agent/infusion and monitored care; do not exceed the regimen ceiling or keep repeating oral tablets.
Once controlled, prescribe the actual oral maintenance dose, BP observation schedule, thresholds for withholding/escalation and delivery/postnatal plan.
Delivery timing depends on gestation, maternal/fetal condition and the underlying disorder; maternal deterioration overrides a plan to complete corticosteroids.

escalation: Stroke symptoms, pulmonary oedema, recurrent severe BP or other end-organ dysfunction: critical-care review immediately.
Track the time severe BP was recognised and the time of treatment/response; hand over all doses and fluids.
postEventCare: Continue frequent BP checks during acute control and after dose changes; symptoms or recurrent severe values need prompt review.
Arrange an explicit postpartum BP/medication review; methyldopa should be stopped within 2 days of birth with a substitute if treatment remains necessary (NICE).

title: Maternal Collapse / Cardiac Arrest
recognize: Unresponsive with absent/abnormal breathing: activate the cardiac-arrest response and start CPR; a trained clinician checks pulse without delaying compressions.
Collapse with a pulse is still an emergency: airway/oxygenation, ECG/BP and urgent cause-directed treatment.
callForHelp: Call cardiac-arrest team, senior obstetrician, anaesthetist and neonatal team; bring defibrillator and resuscitative-birth equipment immediately.
Assign a timer/recorder, uterine displacement and early preparation for resuscitative hysterotomy at the arrest location.

steps: High-quality CPR on a firm surface: 100–120 compressions/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil and minimal pauses; 30:2 until an advanced airway. Use usual adult defibrillation energies.
For a uterus at/above the umbilicus (about ≥20 weeks), maintain MANUAL left uterine displacement during supine CPR. Do not use a tilt that compromises compressions.

Follow the rhythm-specific adult ALS sequence, including adrenaline IV/IO at the correct time and interval. Obtain IV/IO access and secure oxygenation/ventilation without prolonged compression pauses.

Prepare resuscitative hysterotomy immediately and perform as soon as possible by the skilled team at the site of arrest. Do not wait for a four-minute alarm or move to theatre before starting preparation.

investigations: During resuscitation, glucose, blood gas/electrolytes and focussed ultrasound only when it does not interrupt CPR or treatment.

Assess standard reversible causes (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, metabolic/electrolyte disturbance, hypothermia, thrombosis, tamponade, tension pneumothorax and toxins) plus obstetric haemorrhage, eclampsia, sepsis and peripartum cardiomyopathy.

steps: Treat the cause during CPR: rapid haemorrhage control/blood products, PE reperfusion when indicated, anaphylaxis treatment or correction of electrolyte/drug toxicity as appropriate.
Resuscitative birth primarily relieves maternal aortocaval compression; neonatal resuscitation is managed by a separate team.
After ROSC, continue a multidisciplinary post-arrest pathway with oxygenation, ventilation, perfusion, temperature and neurological assessment.

escalation: ICU and cause-specific specialist support after ROSC; consider extracorporeal CPR only within a functioning experienced system.
postEventCare: Document the full timeline, rhythms, shocks, drugs, uterine displacement and birth; maternal/neonatal follow-up and family communication.
Offer team/patient-family debrief and multidisciplinary review.

title: Maternal Sepsis
recognize: Suspected infection with new organ dysfunction: hypotension, altered mental state, oliguria, hypoxaemia, lactate elevation or coagulopathy. Fever can be absent.
Examine for uterine tenderness/foul lochia or retained tissue, urinary infection, pneumonia, wound infection or another source; obstetric early-warning tools support but do not replace assessment.
callForHelp: Activate maternal-sepsis response, senior obstetrician, anaesthesia/critical care and infection/microbiology support; state whether shock is present.
Identify an urgent source-control need and prepare theatre/imaging/intervention in parallel.

steps: Measure lactate, obtain appropriate cultures and bloods BEFORE antibiotics only if doing so causes no substantial delay. Give empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics ideally within 1 h for septic shock/high-likelihood sepsis.

Select treatment for the suspected source, allergies, renal function and local resistance. The complete cards below show named obstetric-infection combinations, not a claim that one antibiotic treats every maternal sepsis source: chorioamnionitis uses ampicillin PLUS gentamicin; postpartum endometritis may use clindamycin PLUS gentamicin; septic miscarriage needs broad anaerobic cover and evacuation.

For hypotension/hypoperfusion, give balanced crystalloid with frequent response/tolerance checks. SMFM recommends 1–2 L in the first 3 h; NICE NG255 uses 500 mL boluses over <15 min with reassessment and consultant review if two boluses fail. Do not apply an automatic unmonitored 30 mL/kg prescription in pregnancy.

If shock persists or fluids are poorly tolerated, start norepinephrine with critical-care supervision, using the explicit salt/concentration/pump calculation below. Catheterise and track hourly urine output; assess oxygenation and perfusion continuously.

investigations: Blood cultures, lactate, CBC/platelets, renal/electrolytes, LFTs, coagulation and blood gas; repeat lactate to assess trajectory.
Urine, genital/wound or respiratory samples as appropriate; ultrasound/CT/MRI according to the suspected source and clinical urgency.

steps: Rapidly remove/control the source: evacuate infected retained tissue, drain an abscess, debride an infected wound or relieve urinary obstruction when indicated.
If the uterus is the suspected/confirmed source, prompt delivery/evacuation may be needed regardless of gestation (SMFM); sepsis alone from another source is not an automatic indication for delivery.

Review antibiotics when microbiology and the clinical response are available, usually within 24–48 h: narrow, adjust renal dosing, stop unnecessary partners and record the total course for the actual infection. Persistent fever/shock requires a search for uncontrolled source or resistant organisms.

escalation: Persistent hypotension, escalating vasopressor need, respiratory failure, altered consciousness, rising lactate or organ dysfunction: ICU immediately.
Assess need for ventilation, renal support and obstetric surgery without waiting for a complete test panel.
postEventCare: Follow organ recovery, glycaemia, fluid balance and medication toxicity; reassess thromboprophylaxis when bleeding/neuraxial constraints permit.
Document a specific antibiotic stop/review date and provide post-sepsis physical/psychological follow-up and counselling.

title: Shoulder Dystocia
recognize: The fetal head has delivered but the shoulders do not deliver with normal gentle axial traction; head retraction/turtle sign may be present.
This is a mechanical birth emergency: drugs do not release the impacted shoulder.
callForHelp: Declare shoulder dystocia and start timing; call senior obstetrician, additional midwives, anaesthetist and neonatal team.
Ask an assistant to record the sequence and announce elapsed time; explain briefly and ask the mother to stop pushing while manoeuvres are organised.

steps: Stop oxytocin and avoid fundal pressure, excessive downward traction or lateral bending of the fetal neck.
McRoberts: assistants hyperflex the maternal hips toward the abdomen; combine with correctly directed SUPRAPUBIC pressure to adduct/rotate the anterior shoulder.

If unsuccessful, a trained operator proceeds to internal rotation (Rubin/Woods/reverse Woods as appropriate) and/or posterior-arm delivery. Episiotomy may make room for a hand but does not itself remove bony impaction.

Change to all-fours when feasible and try the appropriate manoeuvre again. Move between effective manoeuvres promptly rather than repeating forceful traction; allow roughly 30–60 s for an attempted manoeuvre while tracking elapsed time.
If standard manoeuvres fail, the most experienced obstetrician selects rescue options in an equipped setting; these are not routine junior bedside procedures.

investigations: No scan or laboratory test should delay delivery manoeuvres. Record times and call neonatal resuscitation support.

steps: After delivery, hand the baby to the neonatal team for assessment/resuscitation and obtain cord gases when feasible.
Assess the mother for PPH and genital-tract injury, including severe perineal/anal-sphincter injury; treat identified bleeding and injury.

escalation: Failed standard manoeuvres: immediate senior rescue with anaesthetic/theatre readiness.
Neonatal depression or suspected injury: neonatal resuscitation and appropriate NICU/paediatric assessment.
postEventCare: Document head/body delivery times, personnel, traction and manoeuvres in order, and maternal/neonatal findings.
Examine/document newborn limb movement and possible brachial-plexus injury/fracture; arrange follow-up. Debrief and discuss implications for a later pregnancy.

title: Cord Prolapse
recognize: Cord visible/palpable below or alongside the presenting part after membrane rupture, or sudden prolonged fetal bradycardia where prolapse is possible.
Assess fetal heart rate and whether vaginal birth can be safely accomplished immediately; avoid unnecessary handling of the cord.
callForHelp: Declare cord prolapse, call senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, theatre and neonatal team; state fetal heart status and time of diagnosis.

steps: Immediately elevate the presenting part OFF the cord with a gloved hand and keep relieving compression until birth or a reliable alternative is established. Position the mother knee–chest or exaggerated left lateral with head down as appropriate.
Minimise cord handling; do not repeatedly attempt to push the cord above the presenting part. Stop oxytocin.

If transfer/delay is likely, bladder filling can maintain elevation: insert a Foley catheter, instil 500–750 mL saline through the catheter and clamp. This is bladder instillation, NOT an IV fluid dose. Empty the bladder before birth.

Arrange urgent birth: category-1 caesarean with abnormal fetal heart rate unless vaginal birth is imminent and safely achievable. Do not delay birth to complete manoeuvres, tests or transfer paperwork.

investigations: Continuous fetal heart assessment when practical; document the response to decompression. Investigations must not delay birth.

steps: Maintain decompression through transfer/anaesthetic preparation; transfer with an appropriately skilled person when manual elevation is needed.
If full dilatation and rapid safe vaginal birth is possible, the senior operator selects it; otherwise expedite caesarean according to fetal condition.
Tocolysis may be considered by the obstetric team when abnormal fetal heart rate persists and birth is delayed, but must not replace decompression or delay birth.

escalation: Persistent fetal bradycardia: immediate senior operative birth and neonatal resuscitation readiness.
postEventCare: Cord gases and neonatal assessment; evaluate encephalopathy/cooling eligibility if indicated.
Document compression-relief measures, fetal heart changes and decision/birth times; debrief mother/family.

title: Postpartum Seizure (non-eclamptic differentials)
recognize: Any new postpartum seizure is an emergency. Eclampsia can occur later than 48 h and without previously documented hypertension; do not exclude it using that timing alone.
Consider hypoglycaemia, eclampsia/PRES, cerebral venous thrombosis, haemorrhage/stroke, infection, epilepsy, electrolyte disturbance and drug toxicity.
callForHelp: Call anaesthesia/resuscitation, senior obstetrician and neurology/critical care; start seizure timing and record recovery between events.

steps: Protect the airway, position laterally, prevent injury, give oxygen for hypoxaemia and obtain IV access. Check bedside glucose immediately and treat hypoglycaemia.
Treat suspected eclampsia with ONE magnesium regimen even if BP is not currently high, while evaluating alternative causes. Treat severe BP separately when present.

Convulsions lasting ≥5 min or recurrent without recovery need the convulsive-status pathway with airway support. Use the stated benzodiazepine regimen, counting prior doses; persistent status needs a second-line loading agent and ICU.
Labetalol is an antihypertensive, NOT an alternative anticonvulsant. Do not substitute BP treatment for seizure treatment.

investigations: Glucose, CBC/platelets, electrolytes including sodium/calcium/magnesium, renal/LFTs, coagulation and blood gas; infection/toxicology/antiepileptic levels if appropriate.
Urgent neuroimaging for focal signs, prolonged altered consciousness, atypical/refractory seizures or suspected intracranial disease; CT/MRI and venous imaging are chosen for the suspected diagnosis.

steps: Manage persistent convulsions as status: second-line loading, anaesthesia/ventilation when needed and EEG for possible non-convulsive status after motor activity stops.

Confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis, stroke/haemorrhage, CNS infection or epilepsy requires its specific neurology-led treatment; do not start blanket anticoagulation before defining the diagnosis and bleeding risk.
Review magnesium/benzodiazepine exposure, renal function and interacting medicines; use calcium and ventilation for magnesium toxicity.

escalation: Airway compromise, persistent seizures, coma, focal deficit or deteriorating physiology: ICU/neurology immediately.
postEventCare: Monitor consciousness, neurological examination, BP, respiration and recurrence; continue cause-specific treatment and arrange neurological/obstetric follow-up.
Discuss medication implications, driving/local safety restrictions, breastfeeding and recurrence planning once stable.

title: Suspected Ruptured Ectopic
recognize: Possible pregnancy with abdominal/pelvic pain, bleeding, collapse, syncope or shoulder-tip pain; instability/peritonism suggests rupture.
A low/falling hCG or no previously visualised ectopic does not exclude rupture.
callForHelp: Call senior gynaecology, anaesthetist, emergency theatre and blood bank immediately; activate major-haemorrhage support for shock.

steps: ABC, two large-bore IV cannulae, bloods/crossmatch and rapid access to blood. Give emergency uncrossmatched blood when required through the blood-bank policy; do not wait for hCG results to resuscitate.
Perform bedside ultrasound only while the resuscitation/surgical team is being mobilised; unstable suspected rupture proceeds to operative assessment without a prolonged diagnostic work-up.
Keep nil by mouth, monitor closely and prepare emergency laparoscopy/laparotomy according to stability, expertise and resources.

investigations: CBC, blood group/RhD, crossmatch and coagulation/renal tests with quantitative hCG when useful; none should delay surgery.

steps: Obtain surgical haemostasis. Salpingectomy is commonly appropriate; salpingotomy is selected for specific fertility circumstances and requires postoperative hCG surveillance.
Methotrexate and expectant care are NOT treatments for haemodynamic instability or suspected rupture.
Assess contralateral tube/fertility implications and obtain histology as appropriate.

escalation: Continuing shock or haemorrhage: major-transfusion pathway, senior operative control and ICU.
postEventCare: Gestation-specific RhD prophylaxis follows the linked NICE NG126 2026 criteria and confirmed local policy; record eligibility/product/dose rather than a blanket injection for every early loss.
Arrange hCG follow-up when required by the operation/pathology, bereavement support and advice for early assessment in a future pregnancy.

title: Massive APH (praevia/abruption)
recognize: Significant antepartum bleeding with instability or fetal compromise: resuscitate immediately; visible loss can underestimate concealed abruption.
Pain/tender tense uterus suggests abruption; painless bleeding may indicate praevia. Bleeding after membrane rupture with sudden fetal deterioration also raises vasa praevia.
callForHelp: Senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, blood bank, theatre and neonatal team; major-haemorrhage activation when required.

steps: Resuscitate with two IV cannulae, crossmatch/blood, warming and continuous maternal monitoring. Quantify loss and assess shock rather than relying on the pad count.
NO digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded or the senior team is prepared for immediate operative rescue.
Continuous fetal assessment when appropriate; localise the placenta by ultrasound if it does not delay necessary birth. A normal ultrasound does not rule out abruption.

If a preterm birth is likely and time/eligibility allow, choose ONE antenatal-steroid course and consider magnesium neuroprotection using the complete regimens below. Do not postpone urgent maternal/fetal delivery for their completion.

investigations: CBC/platelets, crossmatch, PT/APTT and fibrinogen; blood gas/lactate, calcium and renal function during major loss.
Ultrasound placental localisation/fetal assessment when feasible; RhD status and fetomaternal-haemorrhage testing to guide anti-D under the local gestation-specific policy.

steps: Ongoing major bleeding, maternal deterioration or fetal compromise requires urgent birth and haemorrhage control. Route depends on cause and circumstances; praevia commonly requires caesarean.
Abruption with fetal death and a stabilised mother may favour vaginal birth, but coagulopathy/ongoing bleeding still needs active resuscitation and senior review.
Suspected accreta requires senior specialist planning; avoid forcible placental separation.

escalation: Major transfusion, coagulopathy or persistent shock: theatre, blood-bank/haematology and ICU support immediately.
postEventCare: Monitor for recurrent bleeding/DIC, renal injury and anaemia; send placenta for indicated examination.
Document RhD prophylaxis assessment, neonatal outcome, cause and future pregnancy/birth plan.

title: Massive Pulmonary Embolism
recognize: Acute dyspnoea/chest pain, hypoxaemia, tachycardia, syncope or collapse; hypotension/shock identifies a life-threatening presentation.
Consider haemorrhage, cardiomyopathy, ACS, sepsis and AFE concurrently; pregnancy does not justify delaying objective diagnosis.
callForHelp: Activate senior obstetric, emergency/medical and anaesthetic/critical-care review together; involve PE/cardiothoracic/interventional specialists urgently for shock.

steps: Support airway/oxygenation and circulation; avoid an unmonitored large fluid load in right-ventricular failure. Start ALS immediately if arrest occurs, with manual uterine displacement when indicated.

If VTE is suspected and no strong contraindication exists, give appropriate anticoagulation while arranging expedited objective testing. Stable suspected PE generally uses LMWH; shock, renal dysfunction or likely procedures may favour IV unfractionated heparin.

For life-threatening unstable PE, the expert team decides thrombolysis versus surgical/catheter reperfusion without waiting for a stable-patient work-up. The drug cards below distinguish treatment anticoagulation and the adult alteplase PE regimen.

Check recent birth/surgery, active bleeding and neuraxial procedures before anticoagulant/thrombolytic decisions; in immediately fatal PE, assess risks against the mortality from withholding reperfusion.

investigations: ECG, chest radiograph and baseline CBC/coagulation/renal function; urgent CTPA/VQ testing according to the diagnostic pathway.
Bedside echocardiography may support decisions in an unstable patient when definitive imaging cannot be obtained safely; a normal study does not universally exclude PE.

steps: Treat confirmed PE with the chosen anticoagulant and reassess perfusion, oxygenation and bleeding. Reperfusion is for the appropriate high-risk presentation, not every suspected PE.
After thrombolysis/procedure, restart or adjust heparin according to coagulation results and the documented reperfusion plan; do not automatically give another heparin loading bolus.
Continue pregnancy VTE therapy through pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum, with at least 3 months total treatment; plan birth and neuraxial timing in advance.

escalation: Shock, escalating oxygen/pressor need or arrest: ICU/PE rescue team immediately; consider embolectomy/catheter therapy or extracorporeal support where available.
postEventCare: Provide a written anticoagulant, birth/neuraxial, bleeding and postpartum follow-up plan; consider specialist thrombosis review.
Discuss recurrence symptoms, adherence and future-pregnancy prophylaxis.

title: Massive Transfusion Activation
recognize: Ongoing major obstetric haemorrhage with shock or a predicted rapid substantial transfusion requirement; activate before laboratory confirmation when clinically necessary.
callForHelp: Activate the named hospital major-haemorrhage protocol and identify one clinician to communicate with the blood bank.
Senior obstetrician/anaesthetist leads haemorrhage control and resuscitation; request haematology and ICU support early.

steps: Give emergency red cells when indicated while crossmatched components are arranged. Request balanced component packs under the blood-bank protocol; an adult therapeutic platelet dose is not equivalent to one single-donor component in a literal “1:1:1” count.
Continue source control, TXA for eligible PPH, active warming and rapid access. Monitor delivered products and total fluids; avoid excessive crystalloid dilution.

Measure ionised calcium, potassium, blood gas and temperature repeatedly during rapid transfusion. Replace confirmed/suspected clinically important hypocalcaemia using an explicit calcium prescription and reassess, rather than an undefined “calcium after four units”.

investigations: Serial CBC/platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, blood gas/lactate, ionised calcium, potassium and temperature; viscoelastic testing if locally available.
Use a rapid repeat/result-feedback loop after component replacement; do not wait for the Hb to fall before treating active haemorrhagic shock.

steps: Control the bleeding surgically/obstetrically while blood products restore perfusion and haemostasis.

In ongoing PPH, aim fibrinogen ≥2 g/L with cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen replacement as appropriate; platelets are generally supported to >50×10⁹/L during major bleeding. Guide FFP by coagulation and the major-haemorrhage protocol.
Reassess the need for each component as results become available; monitor for fluid overload, hypothermia, acidosis, citrate-related hypocalcaemia and transfusion reactions.

escalation: Persistent bleeding, acidosis/coagulopathy, hypoperfusion or escalating product need requires immediate senior reassessment of source control and ICU support.
postEventCare: Stop the major-haemorrhage protocol explicitly when haemostasis is achieved; reconcile products, samples and ongoing monitoring.
Assess delayed transfusion complications, anaemia/iron deficit, organ recovery and VTE risk; document and debrief.

title: Uterine Inversion
recognize: After birth: fundus absent/dimpled abdominally or a uterine mass in the vagina/introitus, with pain, bleeding and shock that may be disproportionate to measured loss.
callForHelp: Senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, theatre and blood bank urgently; resuscitation and replacement must proceed together.

steps: Treat shock/haemorrhage with IV access, blood/fluid support and warming; avoid further cord traction. Stop uterotonics temporarily while attempting replacement.
If the placenta is still attached, do NOT remove it before reducing the inversion.

A skilled operator promptly replaces the uterus by sustained pressure toward the umbilicus through the cervical ring, with abdominal counter-support. Do not delay the first attempt for elaborate investigations.
Anaesthesia may be needed for relaxation and repeat attempts; failed manual reduction requires urgent senior operative management.

investigations: CBC, crossmatch, coagulation/fibrinogen and perfusion tests in parallel; do not delay anatomical correction.

steps: After successful reduction, hold/support the uterus until tone returns; then resume/start the prescribed oxytocin regimen and manage residual PPH.
Remove retained tissue only after reduction when appropriate, explore gently, and prescribe indicated prophylactic antibiotics for intrauterine manipulation.
If reduction fails, proceed to theatre for the appropriate surgical reduction; continuing haemorrhage may require additional source control.

escalation: Failure to reduce or continuing shock: immediate theatre/major-haemorrhage rescue and ICU support.
postEventCare: Monitor recurrence, bleeding, uterine tone, urine output and coagulopathy.
Document the reduction/placental sequence and explain recurrence/future-birth planning.

title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism
recognize: Sudden respiratory compromise, hypotension/cardiac arrest and/or major coagulopathy during labour, birth or the early postpartum period; consider AFE alongside haemorrhage, PE, anaphylaxis and other causes.
AFE is a clinical diagnosis; no single laboratory test confirms or excludes it.
callForHelp: Full obstetric, anaesthetic, resuscitation, blood-bank and critical-care response; assign a team leader and family-communication lead.

steps: Support oxygenation and ventilation immediately; if arrested, standard high-quality ALS with pregnancy modifications and early resuscitative-hysterotomy preparation.
Treat haemodynamic collapse with monitored vasopressor/inotropic support guided by physiology/echo; avoid reflex large fluid loads that worsen right/left ventricular failure.
Assess coagulopathy early and activate major-haemorrhage support when bleeding/DIC is present, with fibrinogen, platelets and appropriate components.
Do not delay support while seeking a confirmatory AFE test or administering an unproven “A-OK” drug cocktail.

investigations: CBC/platelets, PT/APTT/fibrinogen, blood gas/lactate, ionised calcium, electrolytes and crossmatch; bedside echo to guide haemodynamic management when available.

steps: Multidisciplinary critical care, haemostasis and cause reassessment; treat ventricular failure, respiratory failure and DIC according to the observed physiology.
Expedite birth when indicated for maternal resuscitation/obstetric reasons; neonatal team provides a separate resuscitation pathway.
Consider mechanical circulatory/extracorporeal support in an experienced centre for selected refractory failure.

escalation: ICU-level care for suspected AFE with cardiorespiratory compromise; early referral to a centre with appropriate circulatory/respiratory support if feasible.
postEventCare: Serial organ-function, coagulation and neurological assessment; coordinated rehabilitation and psychological support for survivors/families.
Document the diagnostic reasoning, timeline and treatments and undertake multidisciplinary review.

title: Anaphylaxis in Pregnancy
recognize: Rapid airway, breathing or circulation compromise after a likely trigger; skin/mucosal changes may be absent.
Wheeze/stridor, swelling, hypotension or collapse demands immediate treatment; do not wait for rash or a tryptase result.
callForHelp: Call resuscitation/anaesthesia and senior obstetric team; bring IM adrenaline, oxygen, IV fluids and airway equipment.

steps: Stop the suspected trigger/infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms immediately; repeat after 5 min for persistent airway/breathing/circulation problems. The complete concentration/volume is below.
Position appropriately: do not allow standing/sudden sitting; in later pregnancy use left-lateral positioning or manual uterine displacement if supine resuscitation is required.

Give oxygen, obtain IV access and support the airway early. Adult shock may need rapid 500–1000 mL crystalloid boluses with reassessment; monitor closely and individualise for cardiac/obstetric physiology.
Persistent features after TWO appropriate IM doses: expert-led refractory-anaphylaxis treatment with a monitored IV adrenaline infusion. Do not give IV boluses of the IM-strength solution.
Antihistamines do not treat airway/breathing/circulation compromise. Routine hydrocortisone is not first-line emergency treatment; neither should delay adrenaline or fluids.

investigations: Monitor ECG, BP, pulse, SpO2 and response continuously. Mast-cell tryptase sampling after initial stabilisation should not delay treatment; arrange timed samples and later baseline under the allergy pathway.

steps: Reassess after every intervention; titrate expert infusion and fluid support for refractory shock. Prepare advanced airway/ventilation if airway oedema or exhaustion progresses.
Assess the fetus after maternal resuscitation; restoring maternal oxygenation/perfusion is the immediate priority.

Choose observation duration by reaction severity and treatment: prolonged observation is required after multiple adrenaline doses, severe respiratory compromise or other high-risk features; do not use a universal 6 h discharge rule.

escalation: Two IM doses with persistent compromise, airway deterioration or shock: critical care and monitored IV infusion immediately.
postEventCare: Record trigger, drug names/doses/timing and severity; provide clear allergy documentation and specialist referral.
Before discharge give emergency advice, an appropriate adrenaline-auto-injector plan/training and follow-up arrangements.

title: Severe Hypo/Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy
recognize: Hypoglycaemia: glucose <4 mmol/L (72 mg/dL); severity is determined by impaired consciousness/need for assistance, not only a <54 mg/dL threshold.
DKA: ketonaemia/acidosis in a patient with diabetes or hyperglycaemia; pregnancy DKA can occur with only modest or normal-range glucose. Measure ketones and VBG when unwell, vomiting or breathless.
callForHelp: Urgent obstetric and diabetes/medical review; DKA, impaired consciousness or haemodynamic compromise requires HDU/ICU capability.

steps: HYPO, awake and safe swallowing: give 15–20 g rapid carbohydrate and recheck after 10–15 min; repeat if still low. If unconscious/unsafe swallowing, give IV glucose or IM glucagon using the exact cards below; never give oral fluids.

DKA: begin monitored isotonic fluid replacement, insulin and electrolyte management with the medical/obstetric team. The usual adult first 1 L over 1 h requires adaptation in pregnancy, cardiac/renal disease or shock; reassess perfusion and fluid tolerance rather than simply prescribing “first litre fast”.

Use SOLUBLE insulin at the stated concentration/rate, not NPH or a pen formulation IV. Measure potassium before and repeatedly during insulin; add glucose early for euglycaemic DKA or when glucose <14 mmol/L.
Continue prescribed basal insulin unless the specialist team changes it. Identify infection, missed insulin, vomiting, steroid exposure or pump failure.

investigations: Hourly glucose and blood ketones; VBG/pH/bicarbonate, potassium/electrolytes, renal function and ECG; initial repeat electrolytes at least at 1 and 2 h, then according to clinical course.
Cultures/other precipitant tests when indicated; monitor fluid balance and fetal condition at a gestation where monitoring informs care.

definitiveManagement.caption: JBDS potassium decisions during DKA — use a monitored prescription
rows: No potassium in the initial replacement fluid; recheck as treatment rapidly lowers potassium.
If passing urine and renal status permits, usual replacement is premixed potassium 40 mmol/L in resuscitation fluid; account for the infusion rate and repeat levels.

Urgent senior/critical-care review for additional replacement and an insulin plan. Do not continue an unreviewed insulin prescription; concentrated potassium requires the appropriate monitored setting.
Never IV push potassium; use premixed/approved dilution and a labelled pump under the hospital policy.

steps: Continue IV insulin until ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND venous pH >7.3 with clinical recovery; glucose correction alone does not mean DKA has resolved.
When eating and transitioning safely, give the appropriate subcutaneous insulin and overlap IV insulin for 30–60 min. Confirm the basal regimen and prevent another missed-insulin interval.
Abnormal fetal monitoring may improve with maternal correction; do not make automatic delivery the treatment for DKA without an obstetric indication.

escalation: Shock, severe acidosis, altered consciousness, hypokalaemia, respiratory compromise or failure of ketones to fall: critical-care/diabetes reassessment immediately.
postEventCare: Review the precipitant and prescribe an explicit insulin plan, ketone/sick-day instructions and hypoglycaemia rescue plan.
Arrange diabetes and obstetric follow-up; verify access to insulin, meters/strips/CGM and ability to use them.

title: Suspected Ovarian Torsion
recognize: Sudden unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting, sometimes intermittent; an adnexal mass increases concern but may be absent.
Normal Doppler flow does NOT exclude torsion. Consider ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis and other surgical causes.
callForHelp: Urgent gynaecology surgical review and anaesthesia; maintain suspicion even with equivocal imaging.

steps: Assess haemodynamics, pregnancy status and differential diagnosis; keep nil by mouth, obtain IV access and provide monitored supportive analgesia/antiemesis.
Arrange ultrasound when immediately available, but do not allow normal Doppler or a delayed scan to postpone surgery when suspicion is high.
Prepare urgent diagnostic laparoscopy with fertility-preserving intent, appropriate consent and surgical support.

investigations: Pregnancy test/hCG, CBC and indicated preoperative tests; pelvic ultrasound is supportive, not a definitive exclusion test.

steps: Detorse and preserve adnexal tissue whenever feasible. In adolescents, ACOG recommends preservation regardless of the dark/blue appearance: colour alone is not proof of irreversible loss.
Cystectomy may be deferred when tissue is oedematous/friable; the surgeon individualises management by age, mass characteristics, fertility goals and malignancy concern.

Do not use a blanket “necrotic-looking ovary = oophorectomy” rule. The cited ACOG recommendation specifically addresses adolescents; adult/postmenopausal decisions need the appropriate oncological/surgical assessment.

escalation: Persistent clinical suspicion: urgent theatre; instability/haemorrhage requires resuscitation and senior surgical control.
postEventCare: Review pathology and arrange follow-up imaging when conservative treatment/cyst follow-up is required.
Explain symptoms of recurrence, fertility implications and the findings/operation performed.

title: Uterine Rupture
recognize: Abnormal fetal heart rate, persistent abdominal/scar pain, loss of station, bleeding, haematuria or maternal shock, especially with a uterine scar/obstruction.
A prior scar or concealed haemorrhage can produce subtle signs; do not wait for all classical findings.
callForHelp: Immediate senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, emergency theatre, blood bank and neonatal team; activate major-haemorrhage support as needed.

steps: STOP oxytocin/prostaglandin administration, resuscitate with two large-bore IV lines and prepare blood.
Immediate laparotomy for suspected rupture with maternal/fetal compromise; do not delay for imaging or a complete laboratory panel.
Continue maternal monitoring, warming and appropriate uterine displacement while preparations proceed.

investigations: Crossmatch, CBC/platelets, coagulation/fibrinogen, blood gas/calcium and renal function in parallel; no investigation delays surgery.

steps: Deliver the fetus and control haemorrhage. The senior surgeon chooses repair versus hysterectomy based on rupture extent, bleeding, tissue condition, stability and fertility considerations.
Inspect for extension into broad ligament, bladder or other structures and obtain additional surgical expertise as required.
Continue balanced haemostatic resuscitation and reassess for coagulopathy/organ injury.

escalation: Ongoing bleeding/shock: major-transfusion and ICU support; neonatal resuscitation and specialist neonatal care.
postEventCare: Document rupture location/extent, repair and future-pregnancy implications; provide a clear specialist birth plan for any later pregnancy.
Assess anaemia, renal/urinary injury, infection, thrombosis risk and psychological recovery; debrief mother/family.
